items.title: Steve Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999
items.q: in that Golden Age you heard the best American music, all the Gershwin, Kern, Duke Ellington, Hoagy Carmichael stuff, all over the world.

ctx.x: Please, not yet. But I would like to see if we could talk a bit about your involvement in jazz music today. Your upbringing in vaudeville with your parents and so forth has been pretty well documented. Can you recall the first kind of music that made an impression on you?

Yeah, there were probably three loose edge stages, counting for the development of my musical tastes and preferences. The first factor is that I was very lucky, given that I would eventually be a composer, a very busy one, even to the present moment, because I grew up in the true Golden Age of American music, and in fact world music. I don’t know how many Americans know this and of those who know it I don’t know how many care, but in that Golden Age you heard the best American music, all the Gershwin, Kern, Duke…

group, they weren’t playing jazz, although one guy was almost in the jazz area, they were just playing songs that they obviously loved to play. And the great majority of them, and this was at the height of the Cold War, when American culture in general was more or less spat upon by the officials there. Nevertheless these guys were playing Golden Age stuff: Irving Berlin songs and George Gershwin songs and Jerome Kern songs. So I had a big smile on my face all through dinner. The food itself wasn’t that great.
